newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Duma dumps welfare cut plans.
newsitem.headline: Russian Duma dumps welfare cut plans.

text.p: The communist-dominated lower house of the Russian parliament turned down a government plan on Tuesday that would have cut a long list of welfare benefits and helped plug a yawning gap in the national budget.

The State Duma rejected a set of draft laws presented by the cabinet, which would slash or cancel social benefits and privileges for war veterans, children, servicemen, police and even legislators themselves to help balance the country's books.
"Since 1992 Russia's social policy has been targeted at raising its share of budget expenditure," Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev told the chamber as he presented the government plan.
"Social expenditure was 27.5 percent of the total in 1992, now it is 45 percent."

The government says that more than 100 million Russians, two-thirds of the population, receive various social benefits, including tax breaks and subsidies on rent and other housing costs exceeding 350 trillion roubles ($60 billion) a year.
"No economy can handle that much," Interfax news agency quoted Sysuyev as saying.
The government is urging cuts in welfare spending to those not in genuine need, saying it should do more for people who are truly struggling in the harsh new world of capitalism.
One of the ministers' main arguments is that the benefits only exist formally on the paper, anyway. The budget cash crunch means those in need are not actually receiving them anyway.
The Duma, dominated by communists and nationalists elected amid discontent about the harsh transition to a market economy, generally opposes most government plans.
But it has tried to avoid head-on clashes with the cabinet for fear of provoking President Boris Yeltsin into calling early parliamentary elections.
The government is cutting planned spending because of a huge undershooting of targeted tax revenues. In the first quarter of the year they fell 41 percent below budget.

Sysuyev said budgeted welfare payments were often unrealistic and have often not been paid. At the end of May pension arrears were 9.5 trillion Russian roubles, while unpaid child benefit amounted to nine trillion.
Russia's 89 regional authorities, which must handle many benefit payments on their own, owed the state 72 trillion.
"We will repay pension debts by June 30 as promised, but if we do not balance the budget we will have the same situation as at the start of the year, with huge debts again," Sysuyev said.

The government aims to remove the burden of benefit payments from regional governments, to reduce the age of children eligible for compensation payments, subsidise only war veterans and not their families and cut parliamentary deputies' expenses.
The reforms to child benefit would save about 26 trillion roubles and another one trillion would come from slashing privileges to those serving in the police and armed forces.
The head of the Duma's Social Policy Committee, nationalist Sergei Kalashnikov, criticised the plan on legal and financial grounds but nevertheless called on deputies to approve it.

On Wednesday, the Duma reviews a government request to cut 1997 budget spending in response to the tax shortfall. Then on Thursday the Duma is scheduled to look at a new tax code. The chamber's budget committee has already recommended rejecting it. ($ = 5760 Russian Roubles)
